articles.title: Inflammation briefly dampens pleasure and the desire to socialize, placebo-controlled study finds
articles.summary: Inflammation may do more than make people feel sick. In a placebo-controlled study, triggering inflammation in healthy women reduced their desire to socialize and ability to feel pleasure, even after accounting for sickness symptoms.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: The psychological motives driving internet justice and public shaming
articles.summary: People who support online public shaming and digital vigilantism are often motivated by the pleasure of seeing others suffer and a desire to boost their own moral status, according to a recent psychological survey.

articles.title: Study finds a specific emotional route from feeling humanized to political compromise
articles.summary: Across five experiments in three countries, people who read posts describing their party as sophisticated rather than as brutes became more open to negotiation — and the emotion doing the work was disgust, not anger or empathy.

articles.title: Estrogen therapy linked to fewer signs of Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue
articles.summary: Women who use estrogen-only hormone therapy during menopause may have a lower risk of developing the brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, according to a large analysis of patient data and autopsy records.

articles.title: Genes may explain about a third of earnings differences, according to a study of 44,500 U.S. twin pairs
articles.summary: A study of 44,500 American twin pairs suggests genetic factors account for nearly one-third of the variation in earnings. But same-sex twins’ tendency to work at the same companies may inflate estimates of how heritable career success is.

articles.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
articles.summary: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

articles.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
articles.summary: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day
articles.summary: A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

articles.title: Your teenage mental health may say something about your vote at 40, study finds
articles.summary: A large 28-year study in Norway reveals that mental health issues starting in adolescence predict distinct adult voting habits. Researchers found early anxiety or disruptive behaviors are linked to specific ideologies and lower trust in government by midlife.

articles.title: Reading for pleasure is linked to better brain health across the lifespan
articles.summary: From early childhood to old age, people who read for pleasure tend to show better cognitive performance and mental well-being. Cambridge researchers argue that reading and book clubs could be low-cost ways to support brain health.

articles.title: Narcissistic parents tend to lean on their children for emotional support, and that is linked to depression later on
articles.summary: When parents cross emotional boundaries and rely on their children as surrogate partners, those children face a higher risk of adult depression. A new cross-cultural study explores the mechanism linking parental vulnerable narcissism to this childhood emotional enmeshment.

articles.summary: A recent experiment reveals that while trendy TikTok videos encourage social media sharing, traditional policy-focused advertisements are far more effective at improving a political candidate's favorability rating among voters.

articles.title: Extreme liberals who rely on traditional sources are the most likely to overrate their science knowledge
articles.summary: People at the political extremes tend to feel more confident about their science knowledge than moderates. But checked against a science quiz, extreme liberals who got their information online were the least likely to overrate themselves.

articles.summary: Patients who received a single dose of mebufotenin improved more on a standard depression scale than those who received a low comparator dose, with most assessed as ready to leave the clinic within two hours.
